prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Once I believed in you; I planted a fig tree. Here, in Vermont, country of no summer. It was a test: if the tree lived, it would mean you existed. By this logic, you do not exist. Or you exist exclusively in warmer climates, in fervent Sicily and Mexico and California, where are grown the unimaginable apricot and fragile peach. Perhaps they see your face in Sicily; here we barely see the hem of your garment. I have to discipline myself to share with John and Noah the tomato crop. If there is justice in some other world, those like myself, whom nature forces into lives of abstinence, should get the lion's share of all things, all objects of hunger, greed being praise of you. And no one praises more intensely than I, with more painfully checked desire, or more deserves to sit at your right hand, if it exists, partaking of the perishable, the immortal fig, which does not travel.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Once, Here, Vermont

outputs.L1: Once, I believed in you; I planted a fig tree here in Vermont, a country without summer. It was a test: if the tree lived, it would mean that you existed. By this logic, you do not exist. Or perhaps you exist exclusively in warmer climates—in fervent Sicily, Mexico, and California—where the unimaginable apricot and the fragile peach are grown. Perhaps they see your face in Sicily; here, we barely glimpse the hem of your garment. I have to discipline myself to share the tomato crop with John and Noah. If there is justice in some other world, those like me, whom nature forces into lives of abstinence, should receive the lion’s share of all things, all objects of hunger—greed itself being praise of you. And no one praises you more intensely than I, with desire more painfully restrained, or more deserves to sit at your right hand, if it exists, partaking of the perishable, immortal fig, which does not travel.
outputs.L2:
I once trusted in your reality, and so I put a fig tree into the ground. I did this in Vermont, a place where summer scarcely exists. The tree was meant as proof: its survival would confirm that you were real. According to that reasoning, you are not. Unless, perhaps, you reveal yourself only in hotter regions—in passionate Sicily, Mexico, and California, where astonishing apricots and delicate peaches can flourish. Maybe your face is visible in Sicily; in Vermont, we catch only the faintest edge of your robe.

I must make myself divide the tomatoes with John and Noah. If another world contains justice, then people like me, condemned by nature to deprivation, ought to receive the greatest portion of everything we crave, since greed itself is a form of devotion to you. No one worships you with greater force than I do, through desire restrained at such cost. No one is more worthy of a place beside your right hand—assuming it is there—where I might eat the fig: mortal yet eternal, and too fragile to be carried elsewhere.
outputs.L3:
The speaker plants a fig tree in Vermont as a personal test of divine existence. If the tree can survive and bear fruit in such an unforgiving climate, it might serve as evidence of God’s presence. Yet the experiment fails: Vermont’s cold weather proves too harsh for the delicate tree. As a result, the speaker begins to doubt that God exists in this barren northern landscape, even while allowing that divine presence may be easier to perceive in warmer, more fertile places.

This doubt gives rise to envy. The speaker imagines regions such as Sicily, Mexico, and California, where figs and other delicate fruits flourish almost effortlessly. In such climates, nature’s abundance seems to reveal divine generosity. Vermont, by contrast, imposes scarcity and restraint. Its inhabitants are forced into a kind of abstinence, not by spiritual choice but by environmental necessity. Even the limited harvest that is available must be shared, making desire all the more difficult to satisfy.

The speaker therefore imagines that such deprivation ought to earn compensation in another world. If earthly life demands self-denial, perhaps the afterlife will provide the abundance that Vermont withholds. The speaker’s restrained appetite becomes more than simple hunger: it develops into an intense form of praise. Desire itself takes on a spiritual quality, sustaining the hope that, beyond this life, the speaker will finally taste an immortal fig—a perfect and everlasting fulfillment of both physical and religious longing.
outputs.L4:
The speaker decides to test faith in God through a simple but demanding experiment: planting a fig tree in Vermont, where the severe winters make its survival unlikely. The tree becomes more than a plant; it is a sign whose success or failure will answer a spiritual question. If it lives and bears fruit despite the hostile climate, the speaker will take that miracle as proof that God exists and intervenes in the world. When the tree fails, however, the result seems to imply either that God is absent or that divine abundance belongs only to warmer, more fertile regions where figs naturally flourish.

Yet the failure does not entirely destroy the speaker’s faith. Instead, Vermont’s coldness and barrenness intensify a sense of deprivation. Because the speaker cannot easily possess the desired fruit, the fig acquires greater value and becomes an emblem of spiritual fulfillment. Hardship deepens longing, and longing preserves the hope that present denial may eventually lead to reward. Thus, although the failed tree appears to undermine belief, it also sustains desire for a future moment of warmth, abundance, and revelation.
outputs.L5:
**Once, Here, Vermont**

Once, the road seemed endless, winding between maple-covered hills and quiet farms. Here, in Vermont, time moved differently—measured by snowfall, woodsmoke, and the slow turning of leaves from green to gold.

At dusk, the mountains softened into blue shadows. A porch light glowed beside a weathered red barn, and somewhere beyond the trees, a river carried the last of the daylight away.

Once, this place had been only a name on a map. Here, it became a memory: cold air, warm cider, and the deep, unmistakable feeling of having arrived.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem in which a failed attempt to grow a fig tree in Vermont becomes a meditation on God’s existence, deprivation, desire, and justice.
counterfactuals.output:
The fig tree arrived in March, a brown wand wrapped in damp paper, while Vermont was still locked beneath its white verdict. I planted it in a clay pot beside the stove and called the bare twig patience. Each morning I touched the soil as if taking the pulse of a small, reluctant god.

By June, it had made seven leaves—green hands opening toward a country they had not chosen. I carried it outside. The hills were extravagant with rain; the rivers shouldered their way through alder and stone. Yet the fig wanted another sun, a longer mercy. It wanted heat stored in walls, dust on the road, wasps entering the purple rooms of fruit. Want, I learned, is sometimes memory without an object.

All summer I fed it. I turned its pot. I praised each new leaf. No figs came.

What proof of God had I expected? A sweetness swelling from wood? A thumbprint of abundance? The poor have always been asked to accept less convincing miracles: broth thinned with water, rent postponed but not forgiven, the child’s shoes made to last one more winter. Blessed are those who hunger, says the book, though the hungry might reasonably ask why blessing so often resembles an empty bowl.

In September the first frost silvered the grass. I dragged the tree indoors, but cold had already entered its green scripture. One by one the leaves yellowed and fell, each with the soft finality of a door closing in another room. I prayed—not well, not faithfully, but with the blunt desire of the deprived: Give me this one thing. Let care be answered by fruit.

The branches blackened.

I kept the dead tree until February. Outside, snow covered the stone walls, the woodpile, the narrow road where the plow passed before dawn. Everything unjust was made briefly beautiful, which is not the same as being made just. Under that clean light, some slept warm and some did not. Some cupboards held summer in jars; some held only their shelves. God, if God existed, was either hidden in the distribution or absent from it.

At last I lifted the tree from its pot. The roots had circled and circled the small dark world allotted to them, seeking an opening the clay would not permit. I thought: perhaps desire is not evidence of fulfillment. Perhaps thirst does not prove a well. Or perhaps the root’s blind turning is the only prayer we are given—the body insisting there must be more earth, even when there is none.

I carried the tree to the compost heap and laid it among coffee grounds, onion skins, the bruised remains of apples. Failure received failure. Snow began again, erasing the path behind me.

In spring I found no resurrection, only rot doing its patient work, feeding what had survived. I do not know if this is God. I do not know if justice waits beneath the frozen ground or must be made by our own ungloved hands. I know only that hunger is holy because it tells the truth: what is absent matters. What we cannot grow here, we can still desire. What we desire, we owe one another.

And somewhere, under a kinder latitude, figs darken on their branches—sweet, innumerable, splitting open in the heat.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a first-person prayer from a cold-climate gardener who envies the abundant fruit of Sicily, Mexico, and California and imagines heaven as a place where the deprived finally feast.
counterfactuals.output:
Lord of seed and season,

Forgive me when I envy Sicily its figs and lemons, Mexico its mangoes and papayas, California its apricots, avocados, and vines heavy with grapes. Here, I kneel in cold soil, counting the brief days between frost and frost, coaxing sweetness from currants, apples, and stubborn roots.

I am grateful for what grows, yet I long for fruit warmed through by a generous sun—for branches bent low with abundance, for juice running over my hands.

So I imagine heaven as Your great orchard, where no one is kept from the table by climate, poverty, distance, or chance. There the deprived feast first. There every hungry child tastes sweetness; every barren season ends; every empty hand is filled. Let me enter beneath those laden trees with wonder, not envy, and share freely what I gather.

Until then, bless my little garden. Make me patient with its limits, faithful in tending it, and generous with its harvest. And keep alive in me the hope of that country where nothing good is scarce.

Amen.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poetic monologue addressed to God, using a dead fig tree, a tomato harvest shared with John and Noah, and the contrast between abstinence and greed as central images.
counterfactuals.output:
God, the fig tree is dead again.

Its branches lift like empty hands,  
gray fingers worrying the air,  
asking what I have not dared to ask:  
whether barrenness is judgment  
or merely another form of waiting.

Beneath it, the tomatoes ripened wildly—  
red lanterns crowded among the leaves,  
each one swollen with August.  
I carried them inside by the armful  
and shared them with John and Noah,  
their laughter bright at the table,  
their knives opening the fruit  
until the cutting board ran crimson  
as though summer itself had a heart.

Teach me why one tree withholds  
while another plant gives beyond measure.

I have praised abstinence, Lord,  
made a virtue of the empty plate,  
the sealed mouth, the untouched cup.  
Yet even fasting can become greed  
when I hunger to be seen as holy.  
And greed—how often it disguises itself  
as gratitude, as gathering, as fear  
that Your earth will close its fist  
before I have taken enough.

John salted his tomato.  
Noah ate his over the sink.  
I counted what remained.

Forgive me.

The dead fig tree kept no fruit for itself.  
The tomatoes kept nothing at all.  
Only I stood between famine and feast,  
trying to possess both:  
the purity of refusal,  
the pleasure of excess.

God, prune this arithmetic from me.  
Let me eat when eating is love,  
abstain when abstinence makes room,  
and never confuse an empty hand  
with a clean one.

If the fig tree lives again,  
I will call it mercy.  
If it does not,  
let its bare limbs still teach me  
how to reach without grasping.

And when the harvest comes—  
red, fragrant, impossible—  
send John and Noah to my door.  
Make me set the whole basket down  
between us.

Make me forget to count.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a passage in the austere, intimate voice of a skeptical believer who searches for divine evidence in gardening and longs for an immortal fig that cannot travel.
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn I kneel beside the fig tree and press two fingers into the soil. It is cool, though the night was warm. I take this for nothing. I have learned not to call every mercy a sign.

The leaves are broad and coarse, like hands made for work. Beneath them, the fruit hangs green and secret. I water the roots. I pull the small weeds that thrive without permission. If God is here, He does not distinguish Himself from moisture, decay, the blind white labor of worms.

Still, I look.

I would like one fig to remain when all the others have split, sweetened, fallen, and been carried off by birds. Not a heavenly fig. Not a symbol. I want its purple weight in my palm, the stem fastened forever to this one branch. Let it be immortal and unable to travel. Let it refuse the mouth, the market, the far country. Let it stay where it was made.

Perhaps this is what I ask of God also: not proof, exactly, but presence without escape.

By noon the soil has dried at the surface. An ant enters a cracked fruit and comes out shining. I watch it go. Then I turn the hose on again, careful not to wash anything away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a prose poem about faith tested through nature: the speaker plants a heat-loving tree in “the country of no summer,” interprets its failure theologically, and argues that hunger itself is a form of praise.
counterfactuals.output:
I planted a fig tree in the country of no summer, where June kept its hands in its pockets and the wind spoke only of distance. I chose the warmest wall, carried stones to its feet, wrapped its thin body in wool. Each morning I searched the branches for green syllables. Each evening the leaves darkened like unanswered letters.

By August, I called its failure a judgment. I had asked heaven for sweetness and received a blackened twig. I said: God is the frost, God is the locked gate, God teaches by withholding. But when I split the bark, a thread of living color shone beneath—so little life it seemed almost ashamed. Then I wondered whether judgment was merely my name for weather, whether faith was not fruit but the foolish act of planting.

Winter came early. The tree stood empty, lifting its bare petitions. No figs, no shade, no proof. Yet below the snow its roots went on desiring what the world refused them: heat, rain, the purple weight of sugar. And I understood that hunger is not the absence of praise. Hunger is praise stripped of music. It is the mouth remembering bread, the root rehearsing summer, the body leaning toward a mercy it cannot manufacture.

So I left the tree where it was. Let the cold test it; let the cold test me. If it dies, the earth will keep the shape of its asking. If it lives, each leaf will be an impossible green amen.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
